messages.subject: regression modeling
messages.body_plain:
Dear R linguists,


I'm modeling two Finnish data sets: one has about 2,000 noun stems, the other about 6,000 noun stems. The response variable is how often the /t/ in the partitive suffix /-tA/ deletes with each stem. Some stems always delete the /t/, other stems never delete it, and yet others vary. (I have a story, but that's irrelevant here.) The response variable varies from 0 to 1. I'll call it del.rate.


I'm attaching scatterplots that show del.rate for both data sets, in two ways. The commands are


plot(data$del.rate)
plot(sort(data$del.rate))

Since del.rate is a continuous variable, it seemed to me that linear regression is appropriate. What worries me is that most of the data are categorical, either invariant deletion or non-deletion. One thing I tried is throwing away all the variable data and fitting a logistic regression model to the invariant subset, but that doesn't seem right either. One reason is that it is the variable stems that are the most frequent. (I believe that is because all the stems are in principle variable, but variation can only be seen with stems that are sufficiently frequent.)

I'm not sure about what is the right thing to do in terms of regression modeling.  Can anyone help?

Thanks!

Arto

Can you treat this as binary, i.e. don't calculate rates for each stem but enter the individual data points with 0 and 1 for a DV of is-there-deletion? Specific stems would be a random factor. (Plus whatever predictors you have as fixed effects.)

messages.subject: Re: regression modeling
messages.body_plain:
One approach to consider: maybe don't reduce the data to del.rate, but
instead model every single occurrence in the corpus as a binary
"does/doesn't delete" case, and use logistic regression to model
probability of deletion.  But what are your predictors?  It sounds like
lexical frequency won't get you all the way there, since you say that
frequency predicts which stems show *variable* deletion.  So if you want to
also account for the difference between stems that are invariantly deleting
or non-deleting, you need at least one other predictor besides frequency.
Perhaps your "story" is not so irrelevant, if it suggests what that
additional predictor should be.
-- dan

Daniel McCloy
http://dan.mccloy.info/

Institute for Learning and Brain Sciences

messages.subject: Re: regression modeling
messages.body_plain:
I would also be interested to see how the # of occurrences in the corpus
correspond to the rates. That is, one would independently suspect that 0
and 1 rates are far more likely when there are few occurrences. And with a
typical Zipfian distribution, the majority of the lexicon will have pretty
sparse #s of occurrences.

Similarly, interested in the 50% cases. I mean, from your graphs it looks
like there are a ton of 1s and 0s, and a sprinkling of >0 and <1, but also
a substantial "line" at 0.5. Are those all items with two occurrences?

In other words, this looks to me like some kind of bi-modal mixture model,
where there is a "low" distribution, with a lot of 0s but then some data
that trails off higher than zero, and a "high" distribution, with a lot of
1s and some points that trail off lower. But then is there also a "mid" (or
maybe "ambiguous" or some other more apt descriptor) distribution that sits
around 0.5? Or is that just an artifact of having a lot of stems with two
occurrences in the corpus? My money would be on the latter, but seems worth
looking at.

Oh wait, just re-read the original message, you already said that the "more
variable" stems (i.e., not just 1 or 0) are the highest occurrence.  So
yeah, that fits my hunch :-)

So I would say you have a couple of options. One would be saying "okay, I'm
going to treat all these words as belonging to one of two classes, deleting
or non-deleting, and I want to know what predicts class membership." There
are more complicated ways to do this, but something simple would be to just
bin all (or almost all) of the stems into those classes, and do logistic
regression. The decision points are (a) whether to include the cases that
are not 0 or 1, and (b) if so, how to categorize them. I could see doing
something like >0.5 and < 0.5, and just drop the exactly 0.5 cases (since
there do not appear to be that many of them; but I'm also assuming almost
all of the 0.5 cases have two occurrences in the corpus).

Another option would be to say, "okay, most stems in this data are 0% or
100% deletion, but what I'm really interested in is how to explain the
variability in the cases that are between 0% and 100%". And then exclude
all the 0s and 1s and try a linear model (and just be sure to inspect the
residuals and perform other standard model checks). Even if you go this
route, though, you still might consider Dan's suggestion to model every
occurrence with a logistic model (instead of aggregating and computing
del.rate over stems). There are pros and cons to both, IMHO.

In short, I think your modeling choice should be driven a lot by the way
you frame your questions, as long as you check to make sure that your
framing makes sense with the data.  As-is, I don't think fitting a simple
linear model is a good way to address either of the above questions. Some
kind of hierarchical mixture model would be a more sophisticated way to
approach the "predicting class membership" question than my binning
suggestion above, but I'm not sure how much the increased sophistication
would buy you, other than a lot more work :-)

cheers,
-scott

messages.subject: Re: regression modeling
messages.body_plain:
(please keep the mailing list in CC)
You misunderstand me.  If your data came to you in aggregated form, then
I'm suggesting that you convert "aatameita 13 aatameja 16" into 33 separate
rows:
aatameita 1
aatameita 0
aatameita 0
aatameita 1
etc

where 16 of the rows are "1" (deletion happened) and 13 are "0" (deletion
did not happen).  Do the same for all stems.  Then your outcome variable is
the column of 1s and 0s, which you can model using regression with a logit
link function: glm(..., family=binomial(link="logit")).  Or if you want
mixed-effects regression, replace glm() with lme4::glmer().
-- dan

Daniel McCloy
http://dan.mccloy.info/
Postdoctoral Research Associate
Institute for Learning and Brain Sciences
University of Washington
